story.title: Liverpool score three at Crystal Palace
story.teaser: Big saves and great goals in a win in London
body: Liverpool won their Premier League match away at Crystal Palace. Alexis Mac Allister, Florian Wirtz and Alexander Isak all scored.
Mac Allister got the first goal with a great header. It was his first Premier League goal of the season. Dominik Szoboszlai gave him the assist with a clever pass.
Wirtz scored next after a good run by Bradley Barcola. It was his first Premier League goal of the season too. Then Wirtz helped Isak score late on. Isak now has seven league goals this season.

Goalkeeper Alisson was the star. He made a stunning save to stop Daichi Kamada, plus lots more important saves. BBC Sport gave him 9 out of 10 and said he was back to his best. Palace did score once, from a penalty.

stories.source_title: Seals long ago evolved to hear above the water — and below
stories.excerpt:
On land, a mother seal can pick out her pup’s cry on a noisy beach. Underwater, seals listen for songs of potential mates or calls warning of predators. This ability to hear well both in and out of the water is unique among mammals. And some marine mammals evolved it nearly 26.7 million years ago, a new study finds.

Seals, sea lions and walruses are known as pinnipeds. They have amphibious hearing — or ears adapted to work well on land and in water. This is “something of a superpower,” says paleontologist James Rule. “They are the only mammals which can do this.” Rule works at Monash Universi

story.title: Seals have super hearing in water and air
story.teaser: How do seals hear so well underwater?
body: Seals can hear well on land and underwater. Scientists have found that their ancestors developed this clever skill nearly 26.7 million years ago.
Seals, sea lions and walruses are called pinnipeds. They are the only mammals that can hear well in both places. Scientist James Rule called it "something of a superpower".

Human ears are filled with air, so we hear badly underwater. Pinnipeds have spongy tissue inside their ears. It fills with blood when they dive. Sound travels well through blood, so they can hear clearly and tell which direction sounds come from.
The team used X-ray scans to look at 217 ears from museums around the world. Some came from fossils of ancient animals. Then the scientists worked out how the ears changed over time.
This special hearing gives many pinnipeds great rhythm. Like parrots, they can copy speaking and singing!

word_to_know.definition: A group of sea animals with flippers, including seals, sea lions and walruses.

story.title: Seals Have a Hearing Superpower
story.teaser: Seal ears work in the air and under the sea. Here's how.
body: Seals, sea lions and walruses can hear well on land and underwater. Scientists say no other mammals can do this. A new study found that some of these animals evolved this skill nearly 26.7 million years ago.
Human ears are filled with air. That works on land, but not underwater. Water is over 800 times more dense than air, so very little underwater sound gets through to our ears.

Seals have spongy tissue inside their ears. When they dive, it fills with blood. This keeps the pressure the same inside and outside their ears. Sound can travel well through blood, so seals can hear clearly underwater.

The team scanned 217 ear specimens from museums with X-rays. They used the 3-D images to see how ears changed over time. The scientists also said loud sounds from boats can change how seals behave, because seals rely on sound to talk to each other.

word_to_know.definition: Samples of animals or plants that scientists keep and study.

story.title: Seals are masters of sound
story.teaser: How do seals hear so well above and below the water?
body: Seals have a special skill that no other mammals share. They can hear clearly both in the air and underwater. On a noisy beach, a mother seal can pick out her own pup's cry. Under the sea, she can hear the calls of other seals.

Now scientists have discovered this skill began almost 26.7 million years ago. A team led by James Rule, a paleontologist in Australia, X-rayed 217 ear specimens from museums around the world. The scans came from 119 mammal species, including all 34 modern pinnipeds.

Pinnipeds include seals, sea lions and walruses. Their secret is spongy tissue inside their ears. When they dive, it fills with blood. Human ears work badly underwater because water is more than 800 times denser than air. But blood is similar to water, so sound travels through it well.

The team found the hearing trait appeared in the earliest sea-dwelling pinnipeds. It probably helped them as they moved into deeper seas. Today it even gives some seals a great sense of rhythm. Like parrots, they can mimic speaking and singing.

word_to_know.definition: Seals, sea lions and walruses, which all have flippers.

Inside their ears, pinnipeds have a spongy tissue. It fills with blood when they dive underwater. Blood is much closer to water in density than air is. So sound travels through it well.

stories.source_title: What can you read into Premier League table after 10 games?
stories.excerpt:
We are now more than a quarter of the way through the Premier League season, with each team having played 10 games.

So what can we read into it?

History suggests the answer is quite a lot.

Last season, for instance, the top two - and two of the eventual bottom three - were in the exact spots at this stage that they in finished six months later.

BBC Sport has a look.

Arsenal are top of the table on 27 points - which is higher than the average number of points (23) champions have after 10 games.

In fact, only four teams have taken more points from their first 10 fixtures than the Gunners,

story.title: What the table says after 10 games
story.teaser: Can history tell us who will win the Premier League?
body: Every team in the Premier League has now played 10 games. That is more than a quarter of the season. BBC Sport looked back at history to see what the table might tell us.
Arsenal are top with 27 points. On average, champions have 23 points at this stage. Only four teams have ever had more points than Arsenal after 10 games, and all four won the league.

But there is a funny twist. The only two teams before that had exactly 27 points at this point both missed out on the title. Brighton are second with 22 points. Manchester City have 21 and Liverpool have 18, so they could still win it too.
Crystal Palace are bottom with seven points. But 14 teams have stayed up after being bottom at this stage.
There is still a long way to go, and plenty of time for things to change.

word_to_know.definition: The team that wins the whole league at the end of the season.

story.think_about_it: If you could pick any team to win the league this season, who would you choose and why?

story.title: What the Premier League table can tell us
story.teaser: After 10 games, history gives some clues about the title.
body: Every Premier League team has now played 10 games. Arsenal are top of the table on 27 points. Brighton are second on 22 points.
History gives some clues about what could happen next. Only four teams have won more points from their first 10 games than Arsenal, and all four went on to win the league.
But nothing is certain. The team top after 10 games have won the title in 15 of the 34 seasons so far. That is less than half the time.
There is hope for teams at the bottom too. Crystal Palace are 20th on 7 points. In total, 14 teams have stayed up after being bottom at this stage.
Last season, 15 of the 20 teams finished within three places of where they were after 10 games. Aston Villa made the biggest jump, from 11th to the top four.

stories.excerpt:
Ever dreamed of flying to the Moon and helping to build a base there?

Well, there are a few things you'll need to do before you can make that dream come true.

Nasa has opened applications for astronauts to help in their next chapter of human spaceflight, so we've been checking out what they're looking for.

The chosen applicants will join the US space agency as they aim to return to the Moon, build a Moon base and lay groundwork for first crewed missions to Mars.

story.title: Nasa is looking for new astronauts
story.teaser: Could you help build a base on the Moon one day?
body: Nasa, the US space agency, has opened applications for new astronauts. The people chosen could help return to the Moon, build a Moon base and get ready for the first crewed missions to Mars.
Nasa says it needs more explorers. It has only 32 active astronauts. "We have far more work than we have astronauts," said Randy Bresnik, commander of the Artemis III mission.
Getting picked is very tricky. The last time Nasa asked for astronauts, more than 8,000 people applied. Only 10 made the final cut.

To apply, you must be a US citizen, so people in the UK cannot try this time. You also need a master's degree in a STEM subject, such as engineering or computer science. You need at least three years of work experience too.
Applications close on 3 December. Nasa expects to choose its new astronauts in late 2027.

word_to_know.definition: Short for science, technology, engineering and maths.

stories.source_title: The swan sanctuary wetland fighting climate change
stories.excerpt:
Most people know rainforests are vital in the fight against climate change, but now scientists say wetlands could be even more important.

Saltmarshes, mangrove swamps and wetlands can absorb carbon "four times faster than trees", according to the charity the Wildfowl and Wetlands Trust (WWT).

Celebrating 80 years since WWT's first wetland bird reserve was founded at Slimbridge, in Gloucestershire, the charity's leaders have called for one million hectares of wetlands to be restored across the world.

Sarah Fowler, CEO of WWT, said: "They are mood-boosting, flood-buffering, water-purifying, i

story.title: The soggy secret weapon helping Earth
story.teaser: Why muddy marshes beat trees at soaking up carbon
body: A wetland bird reserve at Slimbridge, in Gloucestershire, is celebrating 80 years. It was started by a naturalist called Peter Scott. He came there in November 1946 to watch thousands of geese and swans.

Now the charity that runs it, the Wildfowl and Wetlands Trust, says wetlands are a "soggy secret weapon" against climate change. Saltmarshes and swamps can soak up carbon four times faster than trees.
Here is how it works. When big tides wash over a saltmarsh, plants get buried in the mud. Those plants are full of carbon, so it gets locked away.
Slimbridge has helped rare birds too. By 1949, barely 24 Hawaiian geese, called Nēnē, were left. Peter Scott raised some at Slimbridge. Today there are more than 3,000.
The charity wants one million hectares of wetlands brought back around the world. That matters, because 40% of the world's species need wetlands to survive.

word_to_know.definition: A substance found in all living things. Too much of it in the air as a gas makes the planet warmer.

Wetlands include saltmarshes and mangrove swamps. The charity says they can absorb carbon four times faster than trees. Carbon is a gas that adds to climate change. One volunteer calls wetlands a soggy secret weapon.
The world has lost 85% of its wetlands. Yet 40% of the world's species need them to survive. The charity now runs 10 wetland bird reserves across the UK.

It all began when a naturalist called Peter Scott saw thousands of geese and swans at Slimbridge. He helped save the Nēnē, or Hawaiian Goose, when only 24 birds were left by 1949. Today there are more than 3,000.

Today his charity runs 10 wetland reserves across the UK. Wetlands are soggy places like marshes and swamps, and scientists say they could be even better than rainforests at fighting climate change.
That is because wetlands can absorb carbon four times faster than trees. Carbon is a gas that warms the planet, and wet plants bury it safely in the mud.
Wetlands are also brilliant for birds. Scott once saved the Hawaiian Goose, when only 24 were left. Now there are more than 3,000!

story.title: Slimbridge's soggy secret weapon
story.teaser: How a bird reserve became a climate secret weapon
body: Slimbridge wetland reserve in Gloucestershire is 80 years old this year. It began in November 1946, when a naturalist called Peter Scott came to the marshy banks of the River Severn to watch migrating swans and geese.

Scott built hides and towers so people could watch the birds without disturbing them. He also helped save the Hawaiian Goose, or Nēnē. By 1949 barely 24 birds remained. Scott asked for geese to be sent to Slimbridge, but the first two to arrive were both females. Nine chicks were later born there, and now more than 3,000 Nēnē geese live across the world.

Wetlands do more than give birds a home. Scientists say they soak up carbon four times faster than trees. That helps slow climate change. But 85% of the world's wetlands have been lost. The Wildfowl and Wetlands Trust now hopes to restore one million hectares of wetlands. Workers there call wetlands a soggy secret weapon.

stories.source_title: 'I can't believe he is one of us' - inside Salah's life in Trabzon
stories.excerpt:
Back in August, when Mohamed Salah landed in Istanbul after flying in from his holiday in Mykonos, he wore Trabzonspor's burgundy and blue home strip as he stepped out of the plane to be greeted by thousands of fans.

That kit sold out almost instantly. Later that day, as Salah headed to Trabzon in north-east Turkey to complete the formalities of one of the most unexpected transfers after the expiry of his Liverpool contract, he asked one of his entourage what he should wear.

"The same kit," came the response, but Trabzonspor president Ertugrul Dogan advised Salah to wear the black away kit i

story.title: Mohamed Salah's goals light up Turkey
story.teaser: A rock and a street have been named after him!
body: Mohamed Salah, who used to play for Liverpool, is now scoring goals for a Turkish team called Trabzonspor. BBC Sport travelled to Turkey to see how the 34-year-old is getting on.
